name: Tetrapeptide-21

lead: Tetrapeptide-21 is a short cosmetic peptide with the sequence GEKG, used in anti-aging serums for firmer, smoother-looking skin.

Papers describe it as stimulating collagen and the extracellular matrix, the structure that gives skin its firmness. Most published work concerns getting it through the skin: a 2018 delivery study, a 2026 hydrogel study and an in vitro fibroblast study. No human clinical trial of its appearance effects was found.

paras: It is applied in serums and creams as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Because peptides are large, polar and easily degraded, researchers have studied enhancer molecules, carrier systems and elastin-derived hydrogels to improve delivery into skin.
No safety data from human trials were found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug.

angle.text: Used in anti-aging serums for firmer, smoother-looking skin. It is described as stimulating collagen and matrix production in skin cells. Research so far covers skin delivery and cell-culture effects.

lead: Tetrapeptide-21 is a four-amino-acid cosmetic peptide (sequence GEKG) used in anti-aging skincare to help skin look firmer and smoother by supporting the collagen-rich matrix beneath the surface. It is applied topically in serums and creams. Published papers describe it as demonstrating anti-aging efficacy and stimulating collagen [1].

It belongs to the family of cosmetic signal peptides alongside palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), a matrikine launched by Sederma in 2000 and described as boosting synthesis of extracellular matrix molecules [2]. Laboratory work has studied GEKG together with Matrixyl in cultured skin cells [3].

The literature on it is mostly formulation science: peptides are hard to deliver into skin because of their size, hydrophilicity, polarity and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation [4]. No human clinical trial of its effect on appearance was found.

paras: A 2018 study in the European Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences examined enhancer molecules and colloidal carrier systems to improve dermal bioavailability of GEKG, noting that peptide delivery into skin is challenging [4]. A 2026 study in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics designed elastin-derived peptide hydrogels for sustained dermal delivery of tetrapeptide-21 [1]. In the 2018 work, ex vivo experiments on human skin at three incubation times compared a nano-sized microemulsion and enhancers with a standard formulation to see how deeply and in which layers GEKG penetrated [4]. In the 2026 hydrogel study, the hydrogels sustained permeation at 7.5 to 20.9 percent over 72 hours versus 26.6 percent for the free peptide solution, giving slower, controlled release [1].

Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS) is described on Wikipedia as a messenger peptide whose attached fatty chain helps it cross skin lipids, with studies cited including a 2005 report on topical use in photoaged facial skin [2]. Tetrapeptide-21 is marketed in the same category of matrix-supporting ingredients, though Wikipedia's Matrixyl article does not discuss it [2].

A 2025 in vitro study in Molecules examined injectable platelet-rich fibrin together with cosmetic peptides, including Matrixyl, on dermal fibroblast viability and extracellular matrix gene expression [3]. These are cell-culture findings and do not show effects on living human skin. In that study the combination of injectable platelet-rich fibrin with GEKG increased cell viability and upregulated the matrix-related genes COL1A1, FN1 and HAS1 at 72 hours, and more strongly than either treatment alone [3].
No studies found. Related laboratory research on delivery systems and cultured fibroblasts exists [4][1][3].
